Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01In memory of Jeremiah P. Ostriker Jeremiah P. Ostriker (1937–2025) died on 6 April 2025, aged 87. We remember his work on dark matter, galaxy formation and the interstellar medium, and his contributions to teaching and collaboration, by working through his 1964 isothermal-cylinder solution. In memory of Jeremiah P. Ostriker — Princeton University tribute ↗ (14 April 2025). The article describes his scientific contributions and shares recollections from colleagues and former students. Approximate a long molecular filament by a cylinder uniform along its axis. Gravity still balances pressure, as in a star, but changing geometry alters the density envelope and mass limit. Here the tribute takes the form of deriving and using a result, rather than only remembering its name. We follow §III of the original paper. Ostriker’s footnote acknowledges the same solution obtained by Stodółkiewicz (1963); it is also called the Stodółkiewicz–Ostriker solution. Notation and length scales below are chosen for this guide. 02From spherical mass to cylindrical line mass Let r measure distance from the axis, and λ(r) be the enclosed mass per unit length. Line mass is mass divided by length, distinct from volume density or projected column density. Assume a long, static, isothermal, nonrotating cylinder, neglecting ends, magnetic fields and turbulent support. Divide the mass in a segment by its length L. Gravity points toward the axis, perpendicular to it. λ(r)=∫0r2πr′ρ(r′)dr′, dλdr=2πrρ gr=−2Gλ(r)r A cylindrical Gaussian surface has side area 2πrL, so gravity times 2πrL equals 4πGλL. This differs from spherical GM/r². Near a regular centre λ ∝ r², so gravity tends to zero linearly rather than diverging. 03Reduce isothermal balance to one equation P=cs²ρ, cs²dlnρdr=−2Gλr 1rddr(rdlnρdr)=−4πGρcs² Write ρ = ρce−ψ, H = cₛ/√(4πGρc), and ξ = r/H. Regular central conditions are ψ(0) = ψ′(0) = 0. The spherical isothermal Lane–Emden term 2ψ′/ξ becomes ψ′/ξ for a cylinder. ψ″+1ξψ′=e−ψ This is not the spherical solution with a relabelled radius. Geometry changes the growth of Gaussian surface area, leaving a different coefficient in the differential equation. 04Verify the analytic solution and its r⁻⁴ envelope ψ=2ln(1+ξ²8), ρ(r)=ρc(1+r²8H²)−2 a≡√8H, ρ(r)=ρc(1+r²/a²)² ψ′=4ξ8+ξ², ψ″+ψ′ξ=64(8+ξ²)²=(1+ξ²8)−2 Density is nearly constant for r ≪ a and falls as r⁻⁴ for r ≫ a, unlike the r⁻² singular isothermal sphere. The scale a marks a smooth transition rather than an abrupt density boundary. Unlike a profile known only by numerical integration, this closed form can be substituted to verify the equation identically. This also makes it a useful numerical benchmark. 05Infinite radial extent but finite line mass λ(r)=2πρc∫0rr′dr′(1+r′²/a²)²=πρca²r²r²+a² λ(r)=2cs²Gr²r²+a², λcrit≡λ(∞)=2cs²G Increasing central density narrows the cylinder, cancelling ρc from its full line mass. Radius a encloses half that line mass. The total mass of an infinitely long cylinder is still infinite: the finite quantity is mass per unit length. cs²=kBTμmp, λcrit≈16.5(T10 K)(2.33μ) M☉ pc−1 This static cylinder supported only by thermal pressure cannot support a larger line mass. Axial fragmentation, end-driven contraction and magnetic, rotational or turbulent support are separate questions; this one formula does not determine every real filament’s fate. 06Pressure truncation and observational projection Truncating at radius R with external pressure gives a line mass below the limit. Set f = λ(R)/λcrit to obtain the surface-to-central density relation algebraically. R=a√(f1−f), ρ(R)ρc=(1−f)², Pext=cs²ρ(R) The side-on projected column density Σ integrates volume density along the line of sight. For the radially unbounded analytic model, it follows the formula below at projected distance b and falls as b⁻³, not r⁻⁴. A pressure-truncated cylinder has a different, finite line-of-sight integration range. Σ(b)=∫−∞∞ρ(√(b²+z²))dz=πρca2(1+b²a²)−3/2 The panel compares static equilibria. Sliders are not time and do not animate physical contraction. Compare geometry with Bonnor–Ebert spheres and time evolution with LPH/Shu collapse. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed temperature, quadruple central density. How do the critical line mass and the radius enclosing half the full line mass change? Show the answer and reasoning The critical line mass 2cₛ²/G is independent of central density and stays unchanged. The half-line-mass radius a = √8H scales as ρc−1/2 and halves. A narrower, denser cylinder has the same line mass integrated to infinite radius. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide.
